newsitem.title: BULGARIA: SOFIA MAYOR IS LIKELY INTERIM PREMIER.
newsitem.headline: SOFIA MAYOR IS LIKELY INTERIM PREMIER.

text.p: Sofia's respected opposition mayor Stefan Sofianski said on Thursday President Petar Stoyanov had approached him informally to head an interim cabinet until elections in April.
Sofianski said the month-long campaign to remove the Socialists from power had given Bulgarians new motivation and he was hopeful that Bulgaria could now catch up with other ex-communist states.
"We have worked together with Mr Stoyanov for five or six years. We know each other, we cannot expect a formal approach. It is a matter which we have to solve all together," he told Reuters.

The ex-communist Socialists won elections in December 1994 but lost the confidence of the electorate because of their government's corruption and failure to carry out reforms agreed with international lenders.

"Unfortunately, maybe as a nation, maybe as a parliament or a government, we have not succeeded in passing through this transition period, and unfortunately, if we look behind, we see nobody behind us in terms of reform," Sofianski said.

"The last years have been especially bad for the country, with a lot of problems in the government, in parliament, a lot of corruption at high levels of government, and that makes the transition period very difficult."
Sofianski said before Stoyanov appointed a caretaker cabinet, all the country's political forces should first agree on main steps to be taken to get reforms under way.
An economist by training, Sofianski was elected mayor in November 1995. He said if he was appointed premier he would return to the municipality afterwards to complete his term.

His ability to keep the city running smoothly despite deep economic crisis has won him the respect of residents. Last year he visited Moscow to negotiate a barter deal exchanging goods for Russian crude to ensure winter fuel supplies.
When opposition protesters besieged and ransacked parliament on January 10, Sofianski played a prominent role trying to calm tension inside and outside parliament.

The next day, municipality staff and opposition supporters worked together to clean up the debris, clearing wrecked cars and mending smashed windows to remove all traces of the riot. "If only it was so easy to clean our minds," he said.
Sofianski, 45, is married with three daughters. His wife is often seen with him at public functions or in Sofia's jazz clubs, and the whole family took part in his 1995 election campaign.
He is famous for his smiling, affable manner and widely liked by his staff. "We do't want him to become prime minister, he's the best boss we've had," said one municipality employee.
Sofianski is a senior member of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces, currently favourite to win the elections, which he expects to mark a sea change in Bulgarian politics.
"People had no motivation, they have it now," he said.

"If there is something positive in all these events, it is that we changed something in the minds of the people. Now people at least have a certain hope for change. The hope is that there will be no more people like the former communists in the government of the country."
